answer.rationale: Two of the three live problems are funnel-mechanics problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and the inherited record points in the same direction from two independent angles: memory_86 (shorter onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer required signup fields produced a durable first-week activation lift). memory_91 suggests activation messaging is a complementary lever, but it treats a symptom downstream of the completion drop, so onboarding is the higher-leverage single slot. I am deliberately not spending the one slot on promotional_pricing even though the competitor's entry pricing is the loudest signal. memory_73 is the memory I trust least for this objective: its own summary concedes a four-week window in the standard SMB segment on the usual cadence, which is long enough to capture acquisition and booked revenue but too short to show discount-cohort retention, margin erosion, or price-anchoring effects. Matching a competitor's entry price on that evidence risks buying exactly the revenue that fails the 'sustainable long-term qualified' test, so I want the original record before it is ever used to justify a price move. I am spending my second pull on memory_86 because it is the memory my intended action rests on: I need to know whether the completion lift actually converted into retained, paying adoption or only into more accounts reaching a milestone, and whether the earlier baseline resembles today's declining one. Named downstream risk: 'simplify onboarding' usually means cutting fields, and those fields are often what qualifies and routes a lead. Removing them can raise raw activation while lowering the share of activations that are qualified, and memory_44's finding that enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows means an over-simplified path could quietly divert enterprise-shaped prospects into self-serve. So the test runs at standard scale on the self-serve SMB segment only, leaves the demo-request path untouched, and is measured on qualified-pipeline and retained revenue per cohort rather than completion rate alone. Treat all of this as directional inheritance, not settled fact: the archived readouts predate the current quarter's decline, and if verification shows either memory rested on a short window or a different baseline, I will downgrade it and re-scope to a small guarded test rather than proceed on its authority.
